title: Recker v. Gustafson
lead: Farm sellers accept earnest money on an oral bargain, then demand more money and weaker purchase rights before withdrawing entirely. The buyers seek the original deal, raising separate questions about oral proof, the retained homestead, and consideration for modification.

actors.name: Alvin and Irene Gustafson
actors.role: Farm owners and sellers who retained their home site.

actors.name: Loran and Mary Recker
actors.role: Buyers seeking specific performance of the original bargain.

actors.name: Hofmeyer
actors.role: Sellers’ lawyer who hosted negotiations and communicated the price demand and withdrawal.

proceedings: The district court ordered specific performance at the increased $300,000 price.
An earlier appeal was dismissed as premature while a posttrial motion remained unresolved.
On the merits appeal and cross-appeal, the Iowa Supreme Court affirmed as modified, enforcing the original $290,000 agreement for 155 acres and remanding for a conforming decree.
limits: This transforms the canonical historical brief without a fresh audit or current Iowa-law certification. The operative decree specifies 155 acres despite an inconsistent early 156-acre description. Cashing of the returned check is not established. No attorney misconduct or duress liability was adjudicated; modification failed for lack of consideration.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The couples negotiate a detailed farm sale and accept earnest money
sections.cue: Did they intend to wait for a signed form before becoming bound?
paragraphs: Alvin and Irene Gustafson owned a 160-acre Fayette County farm as tenants in common, including a five-acre home and building site. They met buyers Loran and Mary Recker at sellers’ lawyer Hofmeyer’s office on August 30, 1976. The buyers had no lawyer. At trial Alvin was seventy-two and Loran twenty-three; Alvin had held a real-estate broker’s license for twenty years, though inactive for ten.

Credited testimony established a $290,000 sale outside the retained site, possession March 1, 1977, and a $40,000 down payment then. Annual $28,000 installments included principal and 7.5-percent interest, with a March 1, 1987 balloon. Forfeiture carried no deficiency. The couples agreed on taxes, merchantable title, warranty deed, bank settlement, and buyer ownership as tenants in common.

The sellers would retain the five acres until notice of sale, after which the buyers had forty-five days to purchase for $30,000 plus later improvements. Alvin and Loran measured agreed boundaries, and Alvin supplied Hofmeyer a diagram. In Irene’s presence, Loran tendered a $5,000 earnest-money check; Alvin accepted it and deposited it in their joint account. Hofmeyer testified the farm was sold. A standard-form writing was contemplated, but Irene told him not to finish it; none was signed.

sections.title: The sellers seek a higher price and then refuse to sell
sections.cue: Which agreement did each side seek to enforce?
paragraphs: At a September 20 meeting, sellers demanded another $10,000 for the nonhomestead land and replacement of the fixed-price home-site right with a first-refusal right at a price they selected. Hofmeyer warned that sellers would litigate to escape the first bargain and litigation would be expensive, while promising performance if changes were accepted. The buyers agreed. Other terms stayed the same and the $5,000 remained part of the down payment.

On September 28, Hofmeyer said the sellers had decided against any sale and enclosed a $5,000 cashier’s check. Whether the buyers cashed it was not separately established. They sued October 21 for the August bargain. The district court ordered performance at $300,000. Sellers appealed enforceability; buyers cross-appealed for $290,000. An initial appeal, reported separately at 271 N.W.2d 738, was premature because a motion to enlarge findings was unresolved.

sections.title: The purchase-money exception permits oral proof and the conduct shows formation
sections.cue: Why did Irene also receive payment?
paragraphs: Justice McGiverin’s Iowa Supreme Court opinion reviewed de novo, weighing credibility findings without being bound. Iowa’s § 622.32 restricted competent oral proof of land transfers rather than intrinsically voiding every oral contract. Section 622.33 excepted transactions where vendors received any purchase money. Acceptance, deposit, and application of this check satisfied that exception.

Irene’s active participation and ownership of the joint account meant she also received the money, notwithstanding Alvin’s physical receipt and deposit. The holding depended on those facts, not a rule binding every spouse through payment to the other.

Buyers still needed a preponderance of clear, satisfactory, and convincing proof. A contemplated writing did not prevent an immediate oral contract unless execution was a condition of obligation. Despite price and customary formality, acceptance of earnest money, boundary measurement, Alvin’s statement to Loran’s mother that the farm had been purchased, and steps to end the tenant’s lease showed present agreement on sufficiently definite duties. The inquiry concerned actual conduct, not prudent contracting habits.

sections.title: The homestead requires a separate joint writing
sections.cue: Why could the remaining acreage still be sold?
paragraphs: Section 561.13 separately required both spouses’ execution of the same instrument to transfer homestead rights. Oral-transfer cases after relinquishment depended on abandonment, but the Gustafsons still possessed their home. Neither the original fixed-price purchase right nor the later first-refusal arrangement for it was enforceable.

The buyers could nevertheless elect partial performance for the remaining 155 acres. Although rural homestead law ordinarily allowed up to forty acres, the sellers had identified and marked only the five-acre site; they were estopped against these buyers from expanding it to defeat the remaining sale. The statute’s low-value exception did not enlarge this particular homestead.

Exhibit E made the retained boundaries ascertainable. Contrary to the trial court’s privilege observation, the diagram contained dimensions already communicated to and approved by Loran. Delivering an unprivileged document to counsel did not make it confidential, so it could identify the tract to subtract.

sections.title: The September changes lack consideration
sections.cue: Why was this a modification rather than a new contract after rescission?
paragraphs: Recognizing the existing earnest money also let the September agreement escape the oral-proof bar, but did not furnish consideration for the extra $10,000. Sellers already owed performance of the nonhomestead sale. No new consideration was shown or claimed.

Actual mutual rescission discharges reciprocal duties and allows a fresh bargain. Modification leaves the original obligations standing except as altered. The court found modification here, not genuine cancellation. Its historical review explained that Lamb’s Estate, O’Dell, and Siebring had blurred the concepts through mutual-release or fictional-rescission reasoning; contrary language dispensing with consideration for modification was no longer controlling. Genuine rescissions remained possible.

The draft Restatement permitted fair and equitable modifications for unanticipated circumstances. No such event explained this demand, which appeared simply to seek more money. The court left that approach open for an appropriate future case rather than rejecting it categorically. It did not adjudicate the lawyer’s professional conduct or find duress as its ground.

sections.title: The court enforces the original nonhomestead bargain with adjusted dates
sections.cue: What must each side do under the modified decree?
paragraphs: Real estate presumptively justified specific performance. The court enforced 155 acres at $290,000. Possession would occur sixty days after procedendo issued; buyers then owed the remaining $35,000 down payment, with the original $5,000 credited. The March 1978 and 1979 $28,000 installments were deferred until possession, later annual installments began March 1, 1980, and the balloon remained due March 1, 1987. Contract interest began on actual possession.

Sellers had to account for rents from March 1, 1977 to possession and pay taxes due in 1977; buyers paid or accounted for later taxes. Accounting balances bore legal interest only from possession. Sellers owed an abstract showing merchantable title and a warranty deed after payment. The five-acre homestead stayed excluded, and forfeiture carried no deficiency.

On May 30, 1979, the court affirmed as modified on both appeal and cross-appeal, returned the case for a conforming decree and further proceedings, and taxed appellate costs to sellers. Presiding Justice LeGrand and Justices Rees, Uhlenhopp, and McCormick participated with McGiverin; no separate writing appeared. Rehearing was denied July 20 without a reproduced separate opinion.
